# From coastal traces to earthquake histories {#sec-session-03}

**Meeting 3 of 13**

## Central question

When do geological traces discriminate a causal history, and when can different processes produce similar deposits?

## The paper pair

Every citation on this page links to its full record in the [bibliography](../bibliography.qmd), which also lists this meeting's readings with access notes.

**Pairing type:** Discovery claim / diagnostic scrutiny.

Atwater, B. F. (1987). Evidence for great Holocene earthquakes along the outer coast of Washington state. *Science, 236*(4804), 942–944. [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.236.4804.942](<https://doi.org/10.1126/science.236.4804.942>)

Read Atwater in full.

Nelson, A. R., Shennan, I., & Long, A. J. (1996). Identifying coseismic subsidence in tidal-wetland stratigraphic sequences at the Cascadia subduction zone of western North America. *Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 101*(B3), 6115–6135. [https://doi.org/10.1029/95JB01051](<https://doi.org/10.1029/95JB01051>)

Read Nelson and colleagues’ abstract, discussion of diagnostic criteria, and conclusions; the discussant examines the detailed examples.

### Why these papers belong together

Atwater presents evidence for great past earthquakes. Nelson and colleagues examine how to distinguish coseismic subsidence from processes that also occur on passive coasts. This is refinement of the inference, not a blanket rejection of the discovery. [@atwater1987; @nelson1996]

## Prepare before the meeting

Bring a stratigraphic, seismic, or paleoenvironmental interpretation. Separate observations, proxy assumptions, dating uncertainty, and causal claims.

## Discussion questions

1. Which observations are directly measured and which quantities are reconstructed?
2. What would make a peat-mud contact insufficient evidence by itself?
3. What new trace would distinguish competing interpretations?

## One-hour meeting

| Time | Activity |
|:--|:--|
| 0-10 min | Independent first judgments; surface disagreements. |
| 10-25 min | Compare the papers: claim, evidence, assumptions, and limits. |
| 25-45 min | Work through the case exercise below. |
| 45-55 min | Translate the discussion into agent requirements and tests. |
| 55-60 min | Record an output and one unresolved disagreement. |

### Case exercise

Construct an evidence table for suddenness, submergence magnitude, lateral extent, tsunami association, and regional synchrony. Add a plausible nonseismic explanation and identify the additional observation needed to discriminate it.

## Agent-design or evaluation output

Trace-inference worksheet: measurement -> uncertainty -> alternative processes -> discriminating trace -> provisional conclusion.

## Optional extensions

- @satake1996: [Time and size of a giant earthquake in Cascadia inferred from Japanese tsunami records of January 1700](https://doi.org/10.1038/379246a0). Nature (1996). The independent trace that dated the event Atwater inferred: written records from Japan and tsunami modelling, with no Cascadia geology in the argument. Cleland's smoking gun, found in another country's archive.
- @yamaguchi1997: [Tree-ring dating the 1700 Cascadia earthquake](https://doi.org/10.1038/40048). Nature (1997). A third line of evidence, from the rings of drowned cedars, that converges on the same winter. The three papers together show what convergence of independent traces looks like, and how many competences it borrowed; see [meeting 11](11-polymathy.qmd).

**How geoscientists actually interpret.** Measured, not argued.

- @bond2007: [What do you think this is? "Conceptual uncertainty" in geoscience interpretation](https://doi.org/10.1130/GSAT01711A.1). GSA Today (2007). 412 geoscientists interpreted the same seismic section; their interpretations varied with their training and experience. The base rate for the variability the trace-inference mode has to live with.
- @polson2010: [Dynamics of uncertainty in geological interpretation](https://doi.org/10.1144/0016-76492009-055). Journal of the Geological Society (2010). How expert judgment in interpretation moves, drifts, and settles, followed over time.
- @baddeley2004: [An introduction to prior information derived from probabilistic judgements: elicitation of knowledge, cognitive bias and herding](https://doi.org/10.1144/GSL.SP.2004.239.01.02). Geological Society, London, Special Publications (2004). Eliciting geological prior knowledge from experts, and the herding and cognitive bias that come with it.
- @rudwick1985: [The Great Devonian Controversy: The Shaping of Scientific Knowledge among Gentlemanly Specialists](https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226731001.001.0001). University of Chicago Press (1985). The classic close study of how a body of geological knowledge was argued into being, from correspondence and notebooks. The model for reconstructing a trajectory rather than accepting a narrative.
- @currie2018: [Rock, Bone, and Ruin: An Optimist's Guide to the Historical Sciences](https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/11421.001.0001). MIT Press (2018). What the historical sciences, paleontology and geology among them, can know and how they know it, against the pessimism about traces.

## Record after the meeting

Record the evidence for your main claim, what changed your mind, what remains unresolved, and one change to the agent or its evaluation.
